Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: Freeport is a century-old commodity miner rather than a rule-breaking innovator, so it fits Gardner's approach poorly despite strong momentum (+57.5% over 52 weeks to October 26, 2026). Its strengths are scale and assets such as Grasberg and Morenci, not a new category, a beloved brand or a visionary founder.
summaries.buffett: Freeport owns hard-to-replicate copper deposits but sells a commodity at market prices, with earnings that swung from a $(239)M loss in 2019 to $4,306M profit in 2021 and $2,204M in 2025. That cyclicality, low free-cash-flow conversion and a P/E near 32 on trailing earnings make it a weak fit for Buffett's predictable, high-return businesses bought at sensible prices.
summaries.munger: Munger would recognise the cornered resource in long-lived mines and the copper demand from electrification, but would weigh the many ways a miner can be hurt: metal prices, Indonesian politics, and accidents like the September 2025 Grasberg mud rush that killed seven workers. It is understandable but not the kind of wonderful business with pricing power he preferred.
summaries.lynch: Freeport is a textbook Lynch cyclical, whose results follow copper prices; buying works best when earnings are depressed and P/Es look high, and selling when P/Es look low at the peak. Today the trailing P/E is about 32 while consensus sees EPS rising from $1.77 (2025 adjusted) to $3.18 in 2026 and $4.32 in 2027 as Grasberg recovers, so timing in the copper cycle is the key judgement.
summaries.fisher: Fisher favoured companies with growing sales from new products and strong research, and Freeport mostly grows by expanding mines and improving recovery, such as its leach innovation that added 101M lbs of copper in H1 2026. It has a capable long-serving team but limited product development, little pricing power and falling margins since 2021, so the fit is partial at best.
summaries.graham: Freeport fails most of Graham's defensive tests: it lost money in 2015, 2016 and 2019, suspended its dividend for several years (no dividend in 2020), and trades at about 48 times its 2023-2025 average EPS of $1.37 and about 4.7 times book value. It is large and financially sound, but there is no margin of safety on Graham's criteria.
summaries.thiel: Thiel looks for monopolies built on proprietary technology, and Freeport sells an undifferentiated commodity in a market shared with Codelco, BHP, Southern Copper and others. Its edge comes from geology and scale, not a secret or a 10x better product.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on durable growth compounders at reasonable multiples, and Freeport's revenue was roughly flat in the twelve months to June 2026 with growth dependent on copper prices and the Grasberg recovery. Copper demand from AI data centres and electrification is a real tailwind, but a cyclical miner with 1.9% FCF yield is not his typical holding.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller's top-down, liquidity-and-catalyst style fits a copper trade better than most frameworks: realized copper prices rose from $4.54/lb in Q2 2025 to $6.17 in Q2 2026 and above $6.50 in Q3, earnings estimates are rising and Grasberg should approach full capacity by end-2027. The risk is that a macro slowdown or China weakness reverses copper quickly.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith avoids cyclical, capital-intensive businesses without pricing power, and Freeport spends about $4.3B a year on capex, converts little profit to free cash flow ($1,116M in 2025) and has falling gross margins since 2021. It does not fit his 'good companies' test.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Freeport is middling: return on invested capital is about 12.7% and operating income of about $6.9B over the last twelve months gives an earnings yield of about 6.9% on an enterprise value near $99.9B. That is neither cheap nor high-return enough to rank near the top of his screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, skilled and honest managers and reinvestment at high returns, and Freeport scores well only on management continuity. Its returns depend on metal prices and reinvestment in big mine expansions (Bagdad, El Abra) carries cost overrun risk, so it is a weak fit.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bets bought cheaply, ideally in distressed businesses; Freeport's Grasberg setback was a temporary problem, but at $65.16, near 32 times trailing EPS and 4.7 times book, the setback is already priced as a recovery. There is no clear Dhandho-style mispricing at today's price.
summaries.wood: Freeport is not an innovation-platform company and is outside ARK's five platforms, though its copper is an input to energy storage, EVs and AI data centres. Its unit costs are rising, not falling down a learning curve, so it fits Wood's approach poorly.
summaries.ackman: Ackman wants simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with pricing power that are insulated from commodity prices, and Freeport is the opposite on the last two points. Its strong balance sheet and simple story do not offset its dependence on copper and gold prices.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep backed scale-economies-shared businesses whose position strengthens every year, while Freeport sells copper at exchange prices and cannot pass scale savings to customers to win share. It is a long-lived asset owner rather than a compounding business model.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge new markets with technology, and Freeport is a mature, century-old miner. The copper market is large and growing, but Freeport is not creating it.
summaries.nash: Freeport passes some of Nash's tests (TTM operating margin about 27%, institutional ownership near 89%, steady earnings beats and a 75-point scorecard), but it is a commodity producer, one of his zones to avoid. It also fails the instant-kill rule because debt of $9,386M exceeds cash of $4,080M, and a DCF on its own averages values it far below $65.16.
